books.section: Topic 6.10 Development of the Middle Class
Social Criticism in the Gilded Age
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889

stimulus.text:
“The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship.... The contrast between the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the laborer with us to-day measures the change which has come with civilization. This change, however, is not to be deplored, but welcomed as highly beneficial.”

“The best means of benefiting the community is to place within its reach the ladders upon which the aspiring can rise — free libraries, parks, and means of recreation, by which men are helped in body and mind.... Thus is the problem of rich and poor to be solved. The laws of accumulation will be left free, the laws of distribution free. Individualism will continue, but the millionaire will be but a trustee for the poor.... Of such as these the public verdict will then be: ‘The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.’”

(Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889)
stimulus.source_note: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889. Public domain; wording checked against the 1889 issue (archive.org scan) and the Norton Voices of Freedom reprint.

stem: Carnegie writes that “the man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.” What does that line best show about his argument?

options.text: He believed all rich men were criminals who deserved prison
options.misconception: Carnegie was himself rich and defended fortunes; he did not call the rich criminals.

options.text: He wanted the rich to give up all their money at once, immediately
options.misconception: He asks the rich to administer wealth wisely, not to give up everything at once.

options.text: He believed the poor should seize the wealth of the rich
options.misconception: Seizure is nowhere in the essay; the giving is done by the rich themselves.

options.text: He believed the rich had a duty to administer wealth for the public good

rationales.A: Carnegie welcomes great fortunes. Disgrace falls on the man who keeps his fortune to the end, not on every rich man.
rationales.B: The essay asks for wise administration during life, not instant surrender of everything.
rationales.C: The poor seize nothing in Carnegie's picture. The millionaire gives as a trustee.
rationales.D: Dying rich is a disgrace because the rich man failed in his duty: to administer his wealth for the public good while he lived.
rationales.general:
Read the line with the sentence before it.
1. The verdict falls on the man who dies rich, keeping his fortune to the end.
2. The essay's answer is administration during life, not after death.
3. The millionaire is a trustee for the poor, holding wealth for the community.
4. So the line states a duty, not a crime.
Remember: a verdict on one kind of rich man is a claim about duty, not about all rich men.
